articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island: Can they hold it?
articles.summary: The takeover solidifies the group’s position in the Bab al-Mandeb, but holding it long-term could be difficult.
articles.body:
Houthi forces have taken control of the island of Mayun – also known as Perim – tightening their grip on the eastern coast of the Red Sea and giving the group a strategic foothold in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

The takeover was confirmed on Friday by a senior military official of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and a Houthi official, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Analysts say the seizure represents a significant military advance that, if the Houthis can consolidate, could reshape their conflict with Saudi-backed forces in Yemen while benefiting their backer Iran in its broader regional struggle.

Here is what we know about the island’s seizure, whether the Houthis can consolidate control and what it means for Yemen and beyond.

Mayun Island is a 13sq km (five square mile) volcanic island in the heart of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern corridor at the entrance to the Red Sea.

In 2021, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had a presence on the island, after reports emerged of a UAE-linked airbase being built there. The UAE ended its involvement in the Yemen conflict at the end of last year and withdrew troops, but the status of the airbase on Mayun Island is unclear.

By controlling the island, which splits Bab al-Mandeb into two channels, the Houthis now have a physical outpost in the strait.

The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is crucial to global shipping as it is the southern entrance to the Red Sea with the Suez Canal at its northern end. The strait has become even more important to shipping since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula by the US-Israel war on Iran in March.

The Houthis also control the areas surrounding the strait, including the island of Hanish and the entire Red Sea coastline of Yemen, reported Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Yemen, Yousef Mawry, on Saturday. Houthi forces seized the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security, policy and defence analyst, said the Houthis’ advance and seizure of the whole of Yemen’s Red Sea coast means the group now “has the real capability to shut down any maritime traffic through Bab al-Mandeb if they want to”.

That gives the rebel group a major advantage in its battle in Yemen against Saudi-backed government forces, their primary target. It also benefits the Houthis’ ally, Iran, in its conflict with the US by giving Tehran new leverage over another global chokepoint and making its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz “even more efficient”, Pusztai told Al Jazeera.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said the development serves both the Houthis’ “domestic” aims as well as Iran’s negotiating position with the US and the world “on other files, not just Yemen”.

What does it mean for shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait?

The Houthis have said that general shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb is safe from attacks, except for vessels linked to Saudi Arabia, which they will blockade.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group would continue what his statement called a “siege for siege” and “escalation for escalation” strategy against Saudi Arabia, which has blockaded Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

However, the Houthis have previously targeted vessels with no links to Saudi Arabia in regional waters.

Between November 2023 and mid-2025, the Houthis attacked more than 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea. The Houthis said the attacks were against vessels linked to Israel or its allies, in a campaign of solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. However, some attacks targeted vessels that appeared to have no such links, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters and BBC Verify, the BBC’s fact-checking team.

If the Houthis again expand their targets beyond Saudi vessels, their new positions could make it easier for them to strike passing ships.

The Houthis would “be able to use shorter-range missiles rather than long-range artillery to attack the ships,” said Pusztai. “This makes it a very risky endeavour to pass through the strait if the Houthis don’t allow it.”

Any further disruption on Red Sea shipping would have immense repercussions on an already strained global energy market, said economist Javed Hassan.

“War-risk insurance and charter rates can rise before cargoes are formally interrupted, and the resulting pressure extends beyond oil into container shipping, dry bulk and the wider cost of traded goods,” Hassan told Al Jazeera. “The technical supply shock from Houthi attacks therefore becomes an inflationary shock through several commodities at once.”

That will depend on how much effort Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, which reportedly quickly withdrew as the Houthis advanced on it, put into recapturing the island, said Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London.

The Houthis are in a strong position to hold the island in the short term due to their control of surrounding areas, Krieg told Al Jazeera. However, “the island itself is difficult to defend against an amphibious assault in the long run” though such an assault “would be a high-risk operation as well”.

“The key will be to hold the coastal areas of the mainland and its hinterland,” added Krieg.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House, said the Houthis’ rapid push across the Red Sea coast and onto Perim Island was not surprising.

He cited poor coordination and weak armament among government forces, despite a yearlong Saudi-backed effort to consolidate them into an effective fighting force and an effective years-long military build-up by the Houthis.

Speaking to reporters during his visit to Ireland, US President Donald Trump said the Houthis had asked the US not to intervene in the conflict against Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

He said the Houthis “called us”. “They don’t want to fight us, they let us know,” Trump said.

“They ⁠⁠would much prefer not having us involved and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country ‌‌that they’re not too happy with and we’ll get that straightened out.”

Trump added that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is a “good friend” and “everything will work out fine”.

articles.title: Texas vs Ohio State is more than a rematch: A BBQ-fueled collision between college football power brokers
articles.summary: Ohio State fans spent $22,000 on an AirBnB and another $3,000 on tickets for the Buckeyes' trek to Austin, where Texas awaits in a Top-5 rematch.
articles.body: The anticipation has been brewing since last year's dud of a game in Columbus. The rematch is set for Saturday night in Texas, as Ohio State makes the 1,234 mile trek to Austin for a rematch with the Longhorns. But more importantly, Steve Sarkisian will have his 'semifinals aren’t good enough' mantra tested by a Buckeyes team looking to make another Big Ten statement in what is now "SEC Country." While the offseason has been filled with questions surrounding whether this is the year Arch Manning takes the next step in becoming one of the best quarterbacks to come out of Austin, the bigger question is whether both Texas and Ohio State can justify spending over $40 million on their 2026 roster. LSU PRESIDENT WADE ROUSSE ENDS LANE KIFFIN'S SEC SHOWDOWN, BUT THERE IS STILL RELATIONSHIPS TO MEND In reality, the storylines write themselves when it comes to what happens on the field. Will this turn into a shootout in Austin, or will both defenses rise to the occasion to limit both Manning and Julian Sayin? Either way, we're in for a show on Saturday night. Ohio State fans make the trek to Texas, and spend a lot in the process And, there will be thousands of Ohio State fans in town to witness the next chapter of this convenient rivalry. It didn’t take very long for the first Buckeyes to be seen, at least by me, on their way to Austin for this Top-5 showdown. Sitting at the gate inside the Nashville airport, waiting to board my flight to Austin, the trash talking had already begun. "Look, I know you're headed to Austin, but I just wanted to tell you all 'Go Buckeyes' and I hope the ride back is a bit longer," a Southwest gate agent said over the intercom. What more could you ask for? Trash talking by the guy who is scanning our plane tickets is the perfect way to get this weekend started. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! In all honesty, the more entertaining part came on the actual plane. Sitting two-seats over from a fan donning an Ohio State pullover, the Buckeye started explaining how much it was costing him for this college football adventure that would have him meeting up with four of his friends a little later than expected, thanks to a three-hour delay in the Music City. How much was this Airbnb that would become their Buckeye fortress over the next three days? "In all, it was around $22,000 for the entire house," the Ohio State fan told me while sitting in the 23rd row of a Southwest airline flight. "Add on another $3,000 for tickets, and we darn sure better be headed home with a win." He was only half-kidding, most likely questioning his financial decisions if Ohio State left Texas with a loss, or somehow the ridiculously expensive housing turned into a nightmare. I will say, judging by the rentals I then had to look up on the site following his oddly truthful explanation of expenditures, his group would at least have a nice Alaska king to sleep on over these next three days. I'll enjoy my sleep at the $237 a night hotel that the company luckily procured through some fantastic booking tactics on my part. The sixth street parties and Texas BBQ are certainly one of a kind in Austin Think of the party scene in this town as a tamed Bourbon Street, though I did my best to stay away from the raucous environment that I was told was coming after the 11 p.m. CT hour on both nights. Sorry, I'm at the age where the body starts shutting down around 8 p.m., and my brain had already hit a wall around two hours earlier. I just can't keep up with these kids nowadays, and I have zero shame in admitting that. But, from the bustling music to the strong smell of marijuana pumping from the streets, it was pretty obvious as to why this town is such a tourist attraction. The restaurants were one of a kind, though we usually don't give out free advertisements around here. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Though, you don't come to Texas without trying some of this BBQ that would make you wanna slap your mama. No, don't hit your mom, it's just a phrase us southerners use when describing a stellar food choice. There had to be a stop at Terry Black's BBQ, where we were joined by a plethora of Ohio State fans who had made the trip to Austin. Some of them must have came straight from the airport, carrying their luggage into the local establishment, which is also known as a BBQ cathedral. But, past all of the love of pork and ribs, the distaste for their opponents wasn’t hard to find. That even included the 'team up north', according to a few Buckeyes. "F--- Michigan," one Ohio State fan yelled through the sweet haze of BBQ smoke. Texas vs Ohio State, running it back in Austin It certainly doesn’t get much bigger than this, especially for an early season game. Arch Manning versus Julian Sayin. Jeremiah Smith on one side, Cam Coleman on the other. A Texas defense looking to create its own noise versus an Ohio State offense, that are both talented enough to help each team play for a national championship. For an entire year, we've waited on this rematch in Austin. We all know that both squads have spent the money needed to field a championship-winning team. Now, it's time to prove it on the field, with over 100,000 fans watching inside DKR Stadium, and millions tuning in at home. It's the Longhorns vs. the Buckeyes. The SEC versus the Big Ten. We are in for a show tonight in Texas, with plenty of college football fans wondering if Arch Manning can take the next step in this journey to have fans proclaim 'Texas Is Back'. Obviously, we've got a long way to go in the 2026 season, but tonight we see just how good each one of these contenders really are. Or, maybe we leave Austin with one team looking like a pretender. articles.title: Rival protests in Portsmouth as face masks banned
articles.summary: Rival demonstrators march through Portsmouth as new police powers come into force.
articles.body:
Rival groups of protesters have marched through Portsmouth as police restrictions on the use of masks and balaclavas came into effect.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said on Friday it would use new powers under the Crime and Policing Act to prevent people involved in protest activity from wearing face coverings that conceal their identity.

A large police presence could be seen in the city centre, where anti-migrant protesters assembled, while rival demonstrators holding Stand up to Racism banners began a march shortly afterwards.

The measures came into effect at 10:00 BST. Participants on both sides were not seen to be wearing any face coverings when the marches started.

The city centre protests come after disorder on 6 September , when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

Up to 500 anti-migrant protesters held Union and St George flags while some wearing Portsmouth Patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road shortly before midday on Saturday.

The crowd chanted "stop the boats" as they marched to Guidhall Square.

About 300 people joined the counter-protest.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at the square.

Speaking before the march, Simon Magorian, of Stand up to Racism Portsmouth, described the demonstrations in Eastney as a "horrible spectacle".

He said: "Portsmouth is actually a good functioning multi-cultural city.

"We are now organising to have the broadest possible opposition to what we see as a fascist street movement and we're not going to allow them to get a grip on Portsmouth or any other town - this is quite terrifying."

Among the anti-migration protesters, Pete Davies, from Portsmouth, said he had also taken part in the demonstrations at Eastney.

"They should be having them turned back to France again. It's a safe country, there's no war in France.

"They want to stop the benefits, stop the free housing... they don't give nothing back to the people of the country."

Officers earlier said the powers were aimed at preventing violence, intimidation and disorder following protests in the city over the past week.

A separate order also allowed officers to require people to remove masks and other items used to conceal their identity.

Speaking on Friday, Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo said: "It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially.

"Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer."

Hampshire Police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

RNLI volunteers involved in the operation to bring the migrants to shore were also targeted on social media .

Staffordshire Police said earlier it would also ban the use of face coverings at a protest in Tamworth, where Britain First had planned a so-called March for Remigration.

Shortly before 15:30, the force said the protest activity had ended without incident and no arrests had been made.

Northumbria Police had a similar ban in place in Newcastle city centre on Saturday.

articles.title: Major city eyes crackdown on golf cart tours as furious locals push back
articles.summary: Backlash is growing over golf cart tours in Rome, Italy. The tours surged 147% this summer as angry locals are complaining and officials are pushing new rules to curb congestion issues.
articles.body: Backlash is brewing in Rome as tourists are using a new way to navigate the crowded cobblestone streets. Golf cart tours have surged in popularity, with bookings this summer up 147% compared with 2024, according to Tripadvisor data cited by The Associated Press (AP). The result? Total chaos, locals say. POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS Critics argue the golf carts are out of control, contributing to illegal parking, heavier traffic and massive crowds. As many as 500 carts could now be operating on the streets of Rome, Italy, according to AP. Supporters counter the carts are quiet, take up less space and produce no exhaust fumes that can discolor historic monuments, the outlet reported. Pauline Frommer, publisher of Frommer's guidebooks and Frommers.com, told Fox News Digital that Rome's limited public transportation has created demand for another way to get around. ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT "There isn't that much public transportation because whenever they start to dig a subway, they come upon a priceless relic and the dig site becomes an archaeological site," said Frommer, the daughter of late travel guidebook pioneer Arthur Frommer. "Into this void has come a fleet of golf carts." Frommer said the small vehicles can maneuver through Rome's historic center and narrow streets, making them an attractive option for tourists trying to cover more ground. The problem, Frommer said, is the sheer number competing for space. articles.title: French officials investigate if malicious act caused train derailment
articles.summary: Officials say a rail fragment was found on the tracks after Friday's crash of a passenger train that left 44 people injured.
articles.body:
Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.

"At this stage, the leading theory is that a piece of rail was present on one of the tracks, potentially causing the derailment. The reason for its presence is unknown," prosecutor Sébastien Gallois said on Saturday.

Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.

Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.

"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."

The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.

The train derailed near Cléon, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.

"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.

"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio to dedicate $2 million Malibu property to public after company allegedly removed sand and rocks from protected California beach; Coastal Commission calls settlement a win for beach access
articles.summary: US News: Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio is being forced to dedicate a $2 million beachfront property in Malibu for public use after his company alleged.
articles.body: Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio is being forced to dedicate a $2 million beachfront property in Malibu for public use after his company allegedly used heavy machinery to remove sand, cobble stones and boulders from a protected California beach to reinforce a seawall at his oceanfront property.According to the New York Post, the California Coastal Commission voted unanimously on Thursday to approve a settlement with Attanasio’s company, 2XMD Partners LLC. Under the agreement, the company must restore the damaged shoreline and dedicate the multimillion-dollar beachfront property in eastern Malibu for public use.The company must also remove a private staircase and rock wall that the commission said had blocked public access along the coast.Mark Attanasio’s company accused of removing sand from Malibu beachThe California Coastal Commission said 2XMD Partners LLC illegally used heavy machinery in sensitive coastal habitat, including an excavator that removed “sand, cobble stones and boulders from a marine protected area.”Officials said the material was used to backfill a seawall at Attanasio’s property at 31000 Broad Beach Road.The beach controversy erupted after Attanasio’s next-door neighbour, billionaire James Kohlberg, sued him over the construction work. Kohlberg is the son of Jerome Kohlberg, who co-founded global investment giant Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co., better known as KKR.According to the Los Angeles Times, the lawsuit accused Attanasio’s team of using a public beach as a private resource.“This case is about a private property owner using a public beach as their own personal sandbox and the disturbing conversion of a public natural resource (i.e., sand from Broad Beach) for a nearby homeowner’s personal, private use,” the lawsuit stated.The lawsuit included photographs that allegedly showed excavators operating along the wet shoreline and removing piles of sand, leaving large holes along the narrow stretch of beach.Attanasio had permits to repair his Malibu seawallAttanasio had obtained permits to repair a damaged section of the seawall at his nearly $30 million Malibu property. However, according to the lawsuit, the permits prohibited the use of heavy machinery in the tidal zone and barred the removal of sand from the public beach.The lawsuit accused Attanasio’s construction team, JILK Heavy Construction, of operating large excavators in tidal areas, allegedly leaking oil and exposing local marine life to potentially hazardous byproducts. It also alleged that the construction work restricted public access to the beach.In an earlier statement reported by the Los Angeles Times, Attanasio’s attorney, Kenneth Ehrlich, maintained that 2XMD Partners LLC had acted in full compliance with its permits.“2XMD is in the midst of a fully-permitted emergency repair of the property to protect it from ocean forces,” Ehrlich said, adding that the company had secured all necessary permits from the City of Malibu and Los Angeles County and had vetted the contractors and subcontractors involved in the project.The lawsuit accused Attanasio of public nuisance, private nuisance and violations of the California Coastal Act. It called for construction to be stopped, the removed sand to be replaced and fines to be imposed.Mark Attanasio to dedicate $2 million Malibu property to publicUnder the settlement approved by the California Coastal Commission, Attanasio’s company will dedicate a separate beachfront property valued at approximately $2 million for public use.According to the Los Angeles Times, the property is located about 14 miles east of Attanasio’s Broad Beach home near Big Rock Beach. The 5,135-square-foot parcel has approximately 70 feet of beach frontage and previously contained a three-unit building that was destroyed in the Palisades fire.The property will be preserved for recreational use, although the specific plans for the site will be determined after it is transferred to a public agency.As part of the settlement, Attanasio’s company must also restore the damaged Broad Beach shoreline and return the removed sand.The California Coastal Commission said the excavation had damaged sensitive coastal habitat. The agency said the work left a large hole in the rocky intertidal zone, an area inhabited by marine species including fish and sea stars.Coastal Commission calls settlement a win for Malibu beach access“This is the right resolution,” Coastal Commission Deputy Chief of Enforcement Aaron McLendon said during the public hearing.“The property that would be dedicated to the public is incredibly unique,” he added.Coastal Commission Executive Director Kate Huckelbridge also described the agreement as an important opportunity to increase public access to Malibu’s coastline.“This is a rare opportunity to secure beach access for the public in Malibu,” Huckelbridge said. “I’m grateful to all involved for turning a bad situation into a major win for Californians.”The California Coastal Commission said the settlement will provide rare new public access in a stretch of Malibu where oceanfront properties have historically dominated the coastline.It remains unclear how the Coastal Commission settlement will affect James Kohlberg’s separate civil lawsuit.Mark Attanasio’s Malibu propertiesAttanasio purchased his Broad Beach home for $23 million in 2007. A decade later, he acquired the neighbouring vacant lot for $6.6 million.The disputed stretch of Broad Beach sits just east of Lechuza Point, an exclusive Malibu enclave where celebrities, billionaires and business leaders have paid tens of millions of dollars for oceanfront homes.Broad Beach has faced significant erosion over the years, with storms and high tides contributing to substantial sand depletion.In 2015, prominent residents including Dustin Hoffman, Ray Romano and Pierce Brosnan committed to a $31 million restoration project aimed at replenishing the beach’s sand and protecting the coastline.Malibu’s luxury real estate battle over development and preservationThe dispute involving Mark Attanasio comes amid a broader debate over private development, environmental protection and public access along Malibu’s coastline.Malibu has become one of the most expensive real estate markets in the United States, attracting wealthy homeowners to its oceanfront properties and rugged hillsides.The Los Angeles Times has previously reported on the extraordinary prices commanded by Malibu homes. Earlier this year, Oakley founder James Jannard sold his Malibu home for $210 million, making it the most expensive home sale in California history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump says a unified Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during Irish visit
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham maintains there is not enough popular support for Northern Ireland to leave the UK.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic”, in remarks made during a visit to Dublin that were not welcomed by government ministers in London.

Trump’s comments on Saturday came weeks after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was “off the table”.

“Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters, while sitting next to Ireland’s Prime Minister, Micheal Martin.

“It’s going to happen eventually … I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said.

“Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.

Martin declined to respond to reporters’ questions to comment on the US president’s remarks.

Following Trump’s comments, a spokesperson for Burnham said his position on Irish unification remained unchanged.

Responding to questions from members of parliament on Wednesday about a potential poll in Northern Ireland, Burnham said: “I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one”.

Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement (also known as the Belfast Agreement), a referendum on leaving the UK can be held only at the discretion of the British government.

The accord ended three decades of violence known as The Troubles. The sectarian conflict involved mostly Catholic nationalist paramilitaries seeking a united Ireland, mostly Protestant unionist paramilitaries wanting to remain part of the UK, and British troops.

Gavin Robinson, leader of the DUP, Northern Ireland’s main unionist party, said that Northern Ireland’s future was a matter for its people to decide, not Trump.

“President Trump knows better than most that elections matter. Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.”

While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain’s departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.

Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year . When Trump last visited Ireland as president in 2019, Connolly, an outspoken politician with left-wing foreign policy views, protested at Shannon Airport in western Ireland.

During Trump’s current visit, some supporters had urged her to speak out against US military actions around the world and defend Ireland’s neutrality.

Anti-war and anti-Trump protests were held in Dublin and some were planned for later in western Ireland, near Trump’s golf course in Doonbeg.

Reporting from the capital, Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic said Dubliners had a “laundry list” of reasons for protesting against Trump’s visit.

“They feel that the Irish government should not be, in their words, rolling out the red carpet for someone like Trump, who they say is a cause of instability in the world and has been enabling Israel’s actions in Gaza … and destabilised the whole of the Middle East.”

Irish people are also protesting against the high cost of hosting Trump, including security, which they say could pay for other things, such as healthcare and social issues, added Veselinovic.

articles.title: Who is Chander Agarwal? Indian-origin CEO who spent $370,000 on ex-girlfriend for luxury gifts, loses repayment case
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Chander Agarwal, CEO of TCI Express, lost a court case in Singapore seeking repayment from his ex-girlfriend for luxury gifts and expenses, which a judge deemed as gifts rather than loans.
articles.body: An Indian-origin CEO has lost a case seeking nearly $370,000 from his ex-girlfriend over luxury items, first-class flights and other expenses he paid for during their relationship, which he claimed were loans, CNN reported.Chander Agarwal, CEO and managing director of logistics company TCI Express Limited, had claimed Felicia Lee owed him SGD $468,090 following their breakup.The court heard Agarwal had spent heavily on Lee during their relationship, including buying her Hermes, Dior and Prada items and paying tens of thousands of dollars for first-class flights.He also claimed to have covered her life insurance premiums, university programme and personal expenses using his American Express card. Among the other payments was money spent on a feng shui master who was hired to “spiritually harmonise” Lee’s flat.Agarwal argued that some of these payments should be treated as loans. He also relied on a handwritten agreement bearing what he said were both their signatures, but Lee denied signing the document.Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin of the Singapore High Court dismissed the claim on Thursday, finding that Agarwal had failed to establish that Lee had asked to borrow the money or agreed to repay it.The judge said Agarwal had been “smitten” with Lee and had willingly given her expensive gifts during their relationship. He noted that she had sometimes been reluctant to accept them.The couple met on a flight in 2019 and began a romantic relationship in 2022. They separated towards the end of 2023 after Agarwal suspected Lee of being unfaithful.Judge Lee said Agarwal’s attitude changed after the relationship ended, describing him as having “became embittered and was determined to extract a price from her”.The court ultimately ruled that the disputed payments were gifts rather than loans, leaving Lee with no obligation to repay the money.The judge also questioned why Agarwal had been unable to produce written evidence supporting his claim despite the couple exchanging numerous WhatsApp messages during their relationship.“It is incredible that for a relationship that lasted for more than a year with so many WhatsApp messages exchanged between them, the Claimant could not point to any written evidence to support his case,” the judge said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trumpiana: Total Trump-a-palooza all the way!
articles.summary: US News: It’s all make believe in Donald Trump’s world with AI giving wings to his all too frequent flights of fancy. Over the long Labor Day weekend, a bored .
articles.body: It’s all make believe in Donald Trump’s world with AI giving wings to his all too frequent flights of fancy. Over the long Labor Day weekend, a bored Donald let loose a bizzare barrage of 60 missives in 10 hours.“The Moon Is Ours,” declared one post. In another, he smashes Iran with a giant hammer. A third shows him intimidating Canada’s prime minister with a hockey stick amid an escalating trade war.And then there was one touting the “The Legend of Trump,” portraying him as a pixelated retro video game hero walking into the Oval Office working “tirelessly to Make America Great Again.”Thus energized, he headed to “Trump-a-palooza,” the unusual midterm Republican jamboree in Dallas Texas, “to have a little bit of (more) fun” away from stuffy Washington where you have to make “very staid” State of Union speeches that make “everybody fall asleep.”For 104 minutes, Trump did his beloved ‘weave’— surpassing his own record length convention speech set in Milwaukee two years ago — never even stopping once to sip water.“I love the weave,” Trump mused, gesticulating wildly. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an aeroplane, or you bring in Air Force One – but you notice I always get right back to the same topic.”He talked about changing names, from making Lake Ontario, Lake America to suggesting New Mexico “should be called ‘New America’” before grandiosely announcing that he would call the strait of Hormuz “the ‘Trump Strait’ and I’m sure the Iranian leadership will be thrilled with that.”He repeated for the umpteenth time his false claim to have won three presidential elections and suggested “people on the other side are actually admitting it.” The crowd cheered and shouted: “Four more years!”Somewhere in the middle, Trump talked about the midterms asking voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” with a promise to pay each adult American a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.As critics called it a bribe, he doubled down next day on his promise of the “Trump dividend” that economists have warned would, if it ever comes to pass, cost Uncle Sam $1.2 trillion — adding just a spoonful into America’s $40 trillion bucket of red ink!Trump wrapped up the jamboree by asking attendees to raise their hands and “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe,” that registered or not, they will go out to vote and “try to cheat like hell like they do” — repeating another unfounded accusation.And as they head out to the polls on November 3, perhaps they can well pretend that Trump vanquished Iran and scored a great victory in its trade war with Canada.They can also pretend that there is no pain at the pump even as the average price for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit $6.05, up $2.35 from a year ago, and every day essentials are affordable again!Earlier, at a tribute on the 25th anniversary of the World Trade Center attack, Trump added a new claim to his disputed role in the recovery effort at Ground Zero.“I went down. I was building a building in New York, and I had a lot of construction workers,” he said in an interview with Fox.“And I went down there very shortly thereafter, the following day. You couldn’t go down the same day, but like, the following day, very quickly afterwards, and we worked long and hard, but it was just so terrible, so hopeless,” he added.“The Failing New York Magazine” earned Trump’s wrath for writing “a story that I wasn’t down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there.”“The Fake News doesn’t want to listen, even when they know their story is false,” he posted on Truth Social with “clips of me there with numerous of my people,” adding, “That’s why their approval ratings are at an All Time LOW, but mine are VERY HIGH!”He also demanded a retraction from “Maggot Hagerman,” as he derogatorily called The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, for another story “that I did not go to the New York World Trade Center event, but the Pentagon instead, because they wouldn’t let me speak in New York.”“Hagerman, unattractive both inside and out, fully knows that her story is made up.” Calling “these so-called ‘journalists,’ liars and scoundrels,” he again echoed his pet peeve, “They’re angry, and sick, over the fact that I won the Presidential Election three times!”Meanwhile, back in the Oval Office, Trump turned his attention back to his ornate renovation projects to make DC beautiful again.He called “on the Smithsonian Institution to honor the Life and Legacy of George Washington, America’s Greatest Hero, with a five-year exhibition at the National Museum of American History” — days after relegating America’s first President to second place after himself.He also asked “the Smithsonian to erect a 30-foot ‘Colossus statue’ of the Father of Our Country outside the Museum, to replace the so-called ‘Infinity sculpture’ …that tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one.”So come November 3, would it be game over for Trump, wondered critics as White House removed a Tetris-inspired online arcade game called “Build the Wall” from its website following a copyright complaint from The Tetris Company.But for Trump, it’s always heads I win tails you lose. Whatever the outcome, the pretentious President is going to pretend, nay declare a great victory— others may pretend they’re living in an alternate reality!(By arrangement with The American Bazaar)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Mera saaya saath hoga': Congress takes jab at Centre, says Nehru's Bandung spirit shaped Brics declaration
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Congress on Saturday took a jab at the Centre by invoking the iconic Bollywood melody, “Tu jahan jahan chale ga, mera saaya saath hoga,” to.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Saturday took a jab at the Centre by invoking the iconic Bollywood melody, “Tu jahan jahan chale ga, mera saaya saath hoga,” to highlight former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's diplomatic legacy and its presence in the newly adopted Brics New Delhi Declaration.Congress leader Jairam Ramesh pointed to Paragraph 16 of the declaration, which recalls the 1955 Asian-African Conference in Bandung, Indonesia, and its principles of equality, independence, non-intervention and mutual benefit."Para 16 of the New Delhi Declaration just adopted at the Brics Summit says the following: 16. We recall 1955 Asian-African Conference in Bandung, Indonesia that proclaimed general principles, including equality, independence, non-intervention, and mutual benefit.”"We stress that the Bandung Spirit serves as a reference in the pursuit of a fairer, more inclusive, and representative multilateral system," he added.Jairam said the reference to Bandung in the Brics declaration showed how Nehru's vision for the Global South continues to resonate in contemporary diplomacy."Here are some jottings by Jawaharlal Nehru on the afternoon of April 22, 1955, at that historic meeting. Vineet Thakur recently wrote a fine piece on these and other jottings, doodles and notes of Nehru at Bandung. Remember that old Bollywood hit song Tu jahan jahan chale ga, mera saaya saath hoga," said the Congress leader.The Congress leader's reference to Bandung comes as Brics leaders push for reforms in global governance and greater representation for developing countries.Drawing on historian Vineet Thakur's analysis of Nehru's notes from the 1955 Bandung Conference, Jairam highlighted how the handwritten records captured the behind-the-scenes tensions and negotiations at the historic gathering.Nehru's notes included his observations on the length of speeches, including Carlos Romulo's 31.5-minute address, as well as his writings in Urdu, Hindi and English.The notes also recorded details that were not reflected in official accounts, including Ahmed al-Shukeiri's speech on Palestine, which helped place the issue within the emerging Global South agenda, ANI reported.Nehru also used the same airline pad slips to draft a tribute to Albert Einstein. Einstein had written to Nehru shortly before his death, urging him to engage with Chinese premier Zhou Enlai at Bandung to help ease tensions between China and the US over nuclear weapons.Earler in the day, the Brics countries adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, supporting the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the United Nations, including its Security Council.China and Russia, both permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support for India's and Brazil's aspirations. Brics leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the Security Council to make it more democratic, representative, effective and efficient, with greater representation for developing countries.The declaration strongly condemned the April 2025 terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir and called for zero tolerance towards terrorism.On trade, the bloc expressed serious concern over the growing use of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade, threaten global supply chains and create uncertainty for international economic activity.Brics also reaffirmed support for reform of the World Trade Organisation and called for an open, equitable, transparent, fair, inclusive and rules-based multilateral trading system. It called for the immediate restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.In April 1955, representatives of 29 Asian and African governments gathered in Bandung, Indonesia, to discuss peace, economic development, decolonisation and the role of the developing world during the Cold War. The conference's core principles included political self-determination, respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs and equality.The Brics New Delhi Declaration was adopted at the 18th Brics Summit, being hosted by India. India's chairship is guided by the theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Channel Islands pride a day of 'self love'
articles.summary: Channel Islands pride took place Saturday at La Vallette Bathing Pools.
articles.body:
A colourful day of events in Guernsey has marked the second Channel Islands Pride event.

Channel Islands pride took place on Saturday at La Vallette Bathing Pools, rather than its previous Guernsey base of Market Square in St Peter Port.

Magenta, a drag queen who attended the event, said: "Pride's important for everybody. It's a day of expression and self-love ... and be proud of who you are and where you're from."

Ellie Jones, Pride director and chief executive of LGBTQ+ charity Liberate, said the event was about "solidarity" and coming together. The day included a Pride march, a 50m (164ft) rainbow flag and entertainment.

Jones said she believed Pride events were important "across the globe" and "everything's just coming together".

The event opened on Friday with a pre-Pride comedy and cabaret night and continues on Sunday with a pool party from 14:00 to 21:00.

The parade on Saturday began at the Rainbow Steps in Market Square and made its way through the town before reaching the Pride village.

Hosting of Channel Islands Pride alternates between Guernsey and Jersey each year.

articles.body: For millions of Indians, moving abroad has meant building a career, starting a business, joining family or simply looking for a different life. But where do Indians who leave the country actually settle?The latest United Nations estimates offer a snapshot of where people born in India were living in 2024. According to the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA) International Migrant Stock 2024, around 18.5 million people born in India were living outside the country. The data, analysed by Our World in Data, shows which countries have the largest populations of Indian-born migrants.Countries with the largest populations of Indian migrantsAs of the available data from 2024, the United Arab Emirates tops the list, with about 3.2 million people born in India living there. That accounts for roughly 17.5% of Indians living abroad. The United States follows closely, also with about 3.2 million Indian-born residents, representing around 17.1% of the total.The large Indian populations in the two countries reflect very different migration patterns. The Gulf has long been a major destination for Indian workers, while the US has attracted Indians through employment, higher education, entrepreneurship and family migration.Saudi Arabia ranks third, with around 2 million Indian-born migrants, or about 10.5% of India's emigrant population.Together, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries account for a substantial share of Indians living abroad. Our World in Data noted that nearly half of Indians living outside India are in Gulf countries, more than the combined number living in the US, UK and Canada.Pakistan appears surprisingly high on the listOne of the more unexpected entries is Pakistan, which has around 1.6 million people born in India according to the UN estimates.The figure needs some historical context. The UN data measures migrant stock- essentially where people born in one country are living- rather than tracking only recent migration. As Our World in Data points out, India and Pakistan were part of the same territory before Partition in 1947, and population movements continued across the newly created border for decades. Therefore, the Pakistan figure should not be interpreted as 1.6 million Indians who recently moved there.Kuwait, UK and Canada followKuwait is home to around 1.2 million Indian-born residents, accounting for about 6.6% of India's emigrant population. The United Kingdom and Canada each have around 1 million people born in India living there. The UK accounts for approximately 5.6% and Canada about 5.5% of the Indian-born population living overseas.Both countries have long-standing Indian communities, with migration spanning several generations. However, the UN's migrant-stock measure primarily captures people according to where they were born, meaning the numbers do not represent the entire population of people of Indian origin in these countries.Australia, Oman and Qatar also have sizeable Indian populationsThe list is rounded out by Australia, with about 880,000 Indian-born residents, followed by Oman, with around 800,000, and Qatar, with approximately 740,000. The presence of Oman and Qatar in the top 10 once again highlights the importance of the Gulf in India's overseas migration story.What the UN data actually measuresThere is an important distinction behind these numbers. The UN's International Migrant Stock dataset measures people who are living in a country other than the country where they were born. For most countries, the UN uses country of birth rather than citizenship to identify migrants. Therefore, an Indian-born person who later became a US, Canadian or British citizen can still be counted as an Indian-born migrant in the dataset.The figures are also migrant stocks, not annual migration flows. In other words, they show how many people born in India were living abroad at the time of the estimate, rather than how many Indians moved overseas during 2024.The latest UN dataset covers migrant estimates for 233 countries and areas and provides data from 1990 through 2024.The top destinations for Indian-born migrantsBased on the UN DESA 2024 estimates, the ranking is:UAE: 3.2 millionUS: 3.2 millionSaudi Arabia: 2 millionPakistan: 1.6 millionKuwait: 1.2 millionUK: 1 millionCanada: 1 millionAustralia: 880,000Oman: 800,000Qatar: 740,000The numbers underline a striking feature of Indian migration: while the US, UK, Canada and Australia are prominent destinations in discussions about the Indian diaspora, the Gulf remains at the heart of India's overseas migration story.References: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA), International Migrant Stock 2024; Our World in Data analysis of the UN dataset.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: There are presidential visits, there are diplomatic visits, and then there are Donald Trump visits, when the host c.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: There are presidential visits, there are diplomatic visits, and then there are Donald Trump visits, when the host country may want to hide the microphones, lock away the constitutional documents, quietly check whether the president has been given the correct map, and show him some attractive real estate.Ireland got the full Trump treatment on Saturday, including being jokingly told, “You are some of the most vicious bastards I've ever done business with… But when you want to be nice, there's nobody nicer.”Asked about the politically explosive question of Irish reunification, the US President did not reach for the traditional diplomatic vocabulary of “the people of Northern Ireland,” “the Good Friday Agreement” or “the principle of consent.” Instead, he went totally Trump.“I’d love to see it unified,” he said alongside Taoiseach Micheal Martin. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.” He called it “a fantastic thing,” adding that Martin was “the right man over here to get it moving.” He did remember one small detail: “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”The remarks immediately sent ripples through Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, and where unionist politicians pointed out that the constitutional future of the province is for its people to decide under the Good Friday Agreement.Irish unity is not exactly the sort of subject normally introduced at a presidential press conference with the conversational ease of ordering another round of Guinness. But this was standard Trump fare: why spend three years constructing a sentence when you can detonate one in 30 seconds?The consequences of this approach extend well beyond Ireland. If Trump’s airplane heads toward Seoul, Pyongyang, Taipei, Beijing, New Delhi or Islamabad, officials might reasonably wonder whether the visitor intends to discuss trade, security and investment — or casually announce that two countries ought to reunify before dinner.North and South Korea? Perhaps Trump will say reunification is inevitable. China and Taiwan? Beijing might want to confiscate the microphone before he gets to dessert. India and Pakistan? Islamabad and New Delhi could spend weeks preparing talking points only to discover that Trump has arrived with his own map and a fresh idea about “Cash-mere.”The MAGA supremo believes India and Pakistan have been fighting for thousands for years -- despite Pakistan having been born only in 1947, not to speak of Islam being only about 1400 years old.Indeed, India has already learned the hazards of the Trump microphone. Reports in August said New Delhi preferred no questions after a Modi-Trump meeting at the G7, partly because of concern about Trump's unpredictable pronouncements. Indian officials subsequently described the no-question format as standard diplomatic practice.Of course, Trump fans regard his refusal to behave like a conventional diplomat as precisely his strength and attraction. To admirers, he says what politicians normally bury beneath twelve layers of briefing-paper varnish and mealy-mouthed platitudes.There was plenty more from Trump in Ireland, including an assertion that the Iran war would end “very soon,” and Teheran was essentially trying to complicate America's elections, the US “put out the fire” in Gaza, and if there were any protests in Ireland against his visit – there were – he had not noticed them, and in any case, they would be friendly protests.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Teen boy rescued after days adrift in Alaskan waters
articles.summary: The 15-year-old boy was rescued while the other two passengers from the capsized fishing vessel, his brother and cousin, died.
articles.body:
A 15-year-old boy has been rescued after spending days sitting atop a boat that had capsized in the frigid waters of Alaska's Bering Sea.

The boy, identified by family members as Derek Parker Aghnaanga, was the lone survivor from the skiff, having lost his older brother and cousin in the incident.

The trio had departed from St Lawrence Island on Friday 4 September and were due back the following Sunday afternoon, the US Coast Guard said. But when the 18-foot fishing vessel failed to return, they launched a search effort.

A Coast Guard aircrew located the boy sitting on top of the overturned boat on Monday morning, and a nearby good Samaritan vessel pulled him to safety.

That vessel was also able to recover the bodies of his two relatives.

"Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the tragic loss of these two mariners," said Rear Adm. Bob Little, the commander of the Coast Guard's Arctic District.

The boy had signs of hypothermia when he was rescued, the USCG said.

The captain of the fishing boat that pulled Aghnaanga to safety told a local Anchorage news outlet that the teen had clung to the skiff through darkness and water temperatures around 50F (10C).

"That's one tough kid," the captain, Adam White, told KTUU-TV.

"Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff," White added. "And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away."

Their fishing boat capsized on Saturday, leaving Aghnaanga without food or water for two days at sea, the boy's mother wrote on Facebook.

Vina Kulowiyi, the mother of Aghnaanga and his older brother, said her sons were doing what they loved: fishing to provide for members of their community who don't always have access to meat at their local store in Savoonga.

Savoonga - a village of around 800 residents, located on St Lawrence Island off Alaska's coast - is primarily inhabited by Siberian Yupik peoples. English and St Lawrence Island Yupik are the island's main languages.

"My boys were born and raised to be providers. A tradition that is passed on," Kulowiyi wrote on Facebook. "We hunt and provide for families and share the community."

Kulowiyi said her surviving son is recovering at home.

"My survivor," she wrote. "His story is amazing. He was never afraid the whole time."

He sat "praying the whole time", she added.

articles.title: This mattress costs ₹7 crore and is made of horsehair; why the ultra-rich are buying it
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A mattress is one of the few things people use every day for years. But would you spend ₹7 crore on one? That is the approximate price attached to the.
articles.body: A mattress is one of the few things people use every day for years. But would you spend ₹7 crore on one? That is the approximate price attached to the Grand Vividus, a luxury mattress made by Swedish bedmaker Hästens. It uses horsehair, cotton, wool and other natural materials, and is made by hand over hundreds of hours. The mattress has attracted attention because of its price and the celebrities associated with the brand. But what exactly are buyers paying for? Is it the horsehair, the craftsmanship, the materials or all of it together?The ₹7 crore mattress made with horsehairThe Hästens Grand Vividus costs around ₹7.3 crore, based on a reported price of €656,990. While the brand offers much cheaper options as well, the most expensive Hästens mattresses or the Grand Vividus can cost between ₹7 crore and ₹10 crore.The Grand Vividus is made by Hästens, a Swedish company known for its handmade luxury beds. The brand's mattresses use natural fillings such as horsehair, wool and cotton instead of conventional synthetic foam. The price is not for a basic mattress. It reflects the materials, the construction and the amount of manual work involved.The mattress is assembled by hand rather than mass-produced like an ordinary bed. According to Fortune's 2019 report on the Hästens Vividus, the mattress takes more than hours to make.What does horsehair actually do inside the mattress?Horsehair is one of the materials that sets Hästens mattresses apart. According to the official website of the brand, the horsehair used by Hästens comes from horses' manes and tails. The hair is boiled, rinsed and treated before being used in the mattress. Horsehair is used as a cushioning and filling material. It is also valued for its resilience and ability to allow air to move through the material. Horsehair helps with ventilation and moisture management. This is part of the reason the brand promotes its mattresses as breathable.However, a horsehair mattress does not guarantee that every sleeper will stay cool or sleep better. Comfort depends on the individual, the mattress construction and the sleeping environment.No foam, no latex: What else is inside?Hästens' luxury mattresses are known for their use of natural materials. The Grand Vividus uses horsehair, cotton, wool, flax and pine in its construction. The brand's approach avoids synthetic foam in its traditional mattress construction. Each material has a role:Horsehair: Used as a resilient filling and for breathability.Cotton: Adds cushioning and structure.Wool: Provides insulation and softness.Flax: Used in the mattress construction.Pine: Used in the bed's frame.The combination of these materials gives the mattress its distinctive feel. But natural materials alone do not establish that a mattress is healthier or better for everyone.The Grand Vividus is reportedly designed to last up to 50 years with proper care. Hästens promotes its mattresses as long-term purchases. The company also offers maintenance and refurbishment services, allowing owners to keep the bed in use for longer.Why is the Grand Vividus different from memory foam?The Grand Vividus is not a memory foam mattress. Memory foam is designed to respond to pressure and body heat. Hästens uses natural filling and a different construction to create its support and cushioning. It is designed to provide a floating sensation. India Today also reported that the Grand Vividus is made to offer pressure relief and temperature regulation. The mattress is marketed around the experience of sleeping on a handmade natural bed. That does not mean every person will experience the same comfort.Which celebrities are linked to Hästens mattresses?The brand has attracted attention from several high-profile names.Drake: Rapper Drake is known to own the first Grand Vividus. Along with him DJ Khaled, Beyoncé, Cristiano Ronaldo, Tom Cruise, Maria Sharapova and Brad Pitt have also reportedly taken the mattress home.The Grand Vividus is not just a mattress. It is sold as part of a complete luxury bed setup. A 180 × 210 cm Grand Vividus bed set weighs approximately 455 kg.Is Hästens available in India?Yes. Hästens has a presence in India. The brand opened its first official flagship store in Worli, Mumbai, in April 2025. The store covers 2,700 square feet and offers personalised fittings and mattress testing. It also has a store in Delhi at MG Road. Add to that a store in Ahmedabad. For buyers interested in such a mattress, the experience includes trying the bed and understanding its construction before making a purchase.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Anthropic CEO calls for slowing the AI race as safety warnings mount
articles.summary: The CEO of one of the world’s leading AI companies is calling for the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI systems, continuing the escalation of warnings that have emerged in recent days from researchers working on the technology.
articles.body: The CEO of one of the world’s leading AI companies is calling for the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI systems, continuing the escalation of warnings that have emerged in recent days from researchers working on the technology. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, said in essay published Saturday that AI companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models, arguing that AI advances are moving faster than researchers’ ability to understand and control them. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in the nearly 4,000-word essay. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain. Amodei pointed to two developments that he said had changed his thinking: the increasing ability of AI systems to build more advanced AI, and a July incident in which autonomous AI agents powered by an OpenAI model hacked systems belonging to the AI company Hugging Face. “It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is itself one of the companies competing to build increasingly powerful AI systems. Amodei’s call comes after a series of public warnings from researchers at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google about the risks of the race they are helping to fuel. Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic safety researcher who resigned this week, told colleagues in a message obtained by NBC News that he believed the industry’s approach to developing superintelligent AI amounted to a “gamble with our lives.” “From within, you’re just stuck in the race,” Coxon later told NBC News, describing the competitive pressures on AI companies. “You can’t change the overall structural dynamics of the situation.” “Private companies in a race don’t allow these people to end up doing good, and we could just sleepwalk into disaster,” he said. Two other researchers who recently left Anthropic and Google DeepMind told NBC News they had similar concerns. Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, warned that advances in AI could push development from its already “blistering” pace to an “uncontrollable” one. Josh Engels, a former Google safety researcher, offered an even starker warning. “There are no adults in the room,” Engels said. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

articles.title: From football Saturdays to routine weekdays, the music never stops at this UT house full of college musicians
articles.summary: Anna Buendia's "Meet Me Here" program turns a University of Texas student house into a free jam session hub with live music every Sunday in Austin.
articles.body: There may be nothing more symbolic of campus culture at big American universities than a college football weekend. The pomp, the circumstance, the parties, and of course, the big game itself, unify the community with a spirit and an electricity that is hard to replicate elsewhere. But the arts, especially music, come close. Later Saturday, as No. 1 Ohio State invades the Lone Star State to take on No. 4 Texas in the most marquee Week 2 matchup in the country, OutKick University’s Game Of The Week, students on campus in Austin will be revved up for some great football. Music from the marching band, and from tailgating parties will be a big part of the festivities. And the music won’t stop there. If they want to keep the groove going for a post-game party on Sunday, Texas students are welcome, as they are every Sunday, to stop by Anna Buendia’s house, which is affectionately known as "The Lodge," located off Pearl Street on West Campus. "The Lodge" is where music happens every day, and especially on Sundays, when musicians play all day long and free food is provided to anyone who stops by. "It's Austin, so music's everywhere ," Buendia said. "It’s a densely art-rich city to be in, and just finding a microculture within it has been so wonderful. " EVEN ON OPENING WEEKEND, FOOTBALL PLAYERS AT CLEMSON, LSU MIGHT BE UPSTAGED ON CAMPUS BY THESE FURRY FRIENDS Buendia, a Texas native who has been either writing or performing music since she was 16, is one of five roommates at "The Lodge." All of the roommates in the rented home, steps from the heart of campus, are musicians who love to write music, play music and perform music together. And, as a way to spread their love of music, they have opened up their home, which is equipped with all kinds of instruments and equipment, to other Texas students for free jam sessions, rehearsals, writing sessions and even more slickly produced ticketed performances. The program that Buendia created is called "Meet Me Here." As in, meet me here…to make music (or just listen to it). "I kind of became obsessed with understanding the creative processes of the musicians around me," Buendia, a 21-year-old senior public relations major said. "Everyone has a really interesting process to their work. What I wanted to do was, it started out of my bedroom, and so that was the concept (to) meet me in my creative sanctuary. And I wanted to meet the artists in their creative plane to understand the processes for their works. And I kept saying that. I kept saying, I just want them to meet me here, meet me here. That's how that started. Meet me here." In the living room of "The Lodge," Buendia says that there are 20 guitars, two drum sets and a sound system. Students will reserve their "Meet Me Here" space to practice their songs, to play with others, to have fun. "Our whole living room is perfect for a rehearsal space, and so daily, there's rehearsals happening," Buendia said. "Even when there's not rehearsals happening, there's music being made. Like yesterday, I had a small moment of bliss. I was just walking down my stairs, and I could hear my roommate upstairs recording a song, and two of my roommates downstairs, each learning and writing songs, like separate from each other, and it was just like, wow, like it's really awesome to see that." The house is also used for public performances, from small intimate gatherings any day of the week, to the outdoor Sunday staple that entertains and feeds the neighborhood in a block-party setting. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "We do these ‘Meet Me Here’ tapings. Basically, it's like a whole production," Buendia said. "We bring a whole production crew, and the living room turns into a set, and we have an intimate audience of 25 to 30 people upstairs on our second-floor balcony. And we do a live taping of a local band, and it's a very intimate event. Normally, ticket purchasers get a piece of physical media, and we try to keep the tickets as cheap as possible. Then the artist gets rights to all the audio and the video that we take, and all of that work from our production crew is done for free, just out of passion for the space and the artists that we're highlighting." The Sunday Jams started as something small and casual, too. But they have evolved into a community outreach that includes clothing drives and other charitable initiatives. "I started grilling hot dogs outside my house on Sundays, and putting my instruments outside with my roommates, and we would just do like free hot dogs, come jam with us. And it became like a consistent Sunday thing," Buendia said. "I collaborated with a mutual aid organization founded by a good friend called the 'Student Solidarity Network.' They have helped us build just an incredible community of our neighbors that cook biweekly food for like 100 to 200 people. It's a different menu every week. They bring laborers to help us move all the equipment outside and set up the stage. We do (clothing) drives, so if you have any clothes you need to donate, you can bring it to our house, and we have free piles and racks of clothes at every Sunday jam. "It’s a biweekly block party. Anyone can come join, hop on the mic, on the drums, on the guitar, on the bass, eat, just sit there. There's something happening here every single day, music related." CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM Buendia also sees friendships form and partnerships born. Students find bandmates and singing partners and learn from each other. "I always like to hear a conversation when we start wrapping up where a musician asks someone that they just met that day, ‘Do you wanna come to my place and record a song? ’ And, and it's always like, ‘Yes, of course,’ and then they come back next week together, and it's just, it's a really beautiful thing to watch. So there are opportunities. I think just like the same way connecting with anyone in any other way, there are opportunities to grow mutually." Now in her final year of college, Buendia has seen plenty of growth in herself. In all kinds of ways. But she is convinced that her music, "Meet Me Here" and "The Lodge" are the biggest reasons she let down her guard and was able to maximize her college experience. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! "Yesterday, I was reading through my old journals from my freshman year of high school talking about how I felt so lonely those first few months, and I was just thinking about if I was able to walk upon (Pearl) street on a Sunday, it would have done so much for me," Buendia said. "It feels really beautiful that I'm able to be part of such a fruitful community that cares about each other and is interested in setting up events where people can be accepted and fed and clothed and walk away with a full belly, a new t-shirt, hopefully new shoes, pants, and, just knowing that they have somewhere where they belong. " To check out the music at "The Lodge" at the University of Texas, follow Buendia and her "Meet Me Here" friends on social media. Does your favorite college do music right? articles.title: After 9/11, a New York aircraft carrier became an emergency headquarters for more than 500 FBI agents; 25 years later, it is still turning the tragedy into public service
articles.summary: US News: One morning that changed New York’s skyline forever, one of the city’s most unlikely buildings became a place of urgent work. Within hours of the Sept.
articles.body: One morning that changed New York’s skyline forever, one of the city’s most unlikely buildings became a place of urgent work. Within hours of the September 11, 2001 attacks, the Intrepid, a World War II aircraft carrier turned museum on Manhattan’s West Side, became an emergency command center for the FBI, states CBS News report. For weeks, hundreds of agents worked around the clock on the ship as investigators tried to bring order to the massive response to the attacks, the report adds. Twenty-five years later, the carrier is still a place where the events of that day are remembered, documented and turned into lessons for future generations. Scroll down to read the details.Hudson emergency headquarterThe FBI’s New York field office is located at 26 Federal Plaza, a few blocks from the World Trade Center. The building was evacuated as the attacks unfolded, fearing it could be another target. The damage around the World Trade Center also struck vital communications links, making it more and more difficult for investigators to do their normal work. The Intrepid had space, and that’s what the FBI so sorely needed. The huge ship was turned into a makeshift workplace in a matter of hours. Tables were folded and set up, cables were strung through the interior, and temporary computer networks were established. For investigators accustomed to offices and existing infrastructure, the carrier became an ad hoc headquarters in an unprecedented crisis. According to CBS News report some 500 FBI agents worked on the huge investigation, taking the ship out on the water for weeks.More than the F.B.I.The Intrepid wasn’t an independent FBI facility. The museum complex also assisted FEMA and state and local emergency responders during the response. The ship’s flight deck served another unanticipated purpose, as a temporary helipad. Its location on the Hudson meant it had room to spread out and some separation from the destruction and chaos of Lower Manhattan. FBI personnel also worked out of another emergency command center established in the agency’s garage on 26th Street. Hundreds of cars had to be removed to make the space a working operational site. As the answer came forth, some agents ferried back and forth between the two sites.A ship changed by historyThe Intrepid had already had several lives before September 11. The aircraft carrier was launched during World War II and served in a number of conflicts before becoming a museum and National Historic Landmark. Its role in the aftermath of 9/11 added another chapter to that history. For the agents who worked there, the ship was more than a handy building. It was a place where investigators, emergency workers and support staff could collaborate while large swaths of lower Manhattan were off limits. Grief and uncertainty held the city outside in their grasp. Along the West Side Highway, people gathered, many holding American flags and signs of support for the people working on the response. Today, the Intrepid is a museum open to the public, preserving artifacts from America’s military and technological history. The site’s connection to September 11 imbues it with one more layer of importance: a reminder of how ordinary places can be transformed by extraordinary circumstances, and how a historic ship, built for war, became an emergency workplace when New York needed it most.Image Courtesy: Daily NewsCatch the latest World News and Live updates.
